Without proper screening and care, severe maternal distress can lead to poor self care, self harm, suicide, impaired mother baby bonding, infant undernutrition, and long term developmental challenges for the child.
source: Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Synthesis

content: Temporary mood changes after childbirth, known as the baby blues, affect up to eighty percent of new mothers due to rapid hormone shifts, usually resolving within two weeks without treatment. If a mother has a sad mood, trouble concentrating, loss of joy, or difficulty bonding persists beyond two weeks, it indicates perinatal depression. Depression affects up to twenty percent of pregnant and postpartum women, with onset occurring before pregnancy in twenty seven percent of cases, during pregnancy in thirty three percent, and after birth in forty percent. Women with long term low mood, known as dysthymia, face higher risks of severe depressive episodes during pregnancy and postpartum.
source: Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Synthesis

content: Maternal anxiety disorders affect about twenty percent of pregnant and postpartum women, causing constant worry, a fast heart rate, feeling restless, and severe trouble sleeping. Perinatal obsessive compulsive disorder affects eight percent of pregnant women and seventeen percent of new mothers after birth. Almost all new mothers have scary, unwanted thoughts about bad things happening to their baby, which is a normal reaction to stress. Unlike psychosis where a person loses touch with reality, mothers with obsessive compulsive disorder stay completely in control of their actions and have no desire or intention to hurt their child.
source: Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Synthesis

content: Bipolar disorder causes major mood swings between deep sadness and high energy. During high energy periods, a woman may need very little sleep, feel hyperactive, and make risky decisions. Over half of women with bipolar disorder experience mood changes during pregnancy or after giving birth. Bipolar type one carries the highest risk for postpartum psychosis, a rare medical emergency that affects about one in every thousand mothers. Postpartum psychosis usually starts suddenly in the first two weeks after birth, causing severe confusion, strange beliefs, and a break from reality that puts both mother and baby in immediate danger.
source: Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Synthesis

content: A traumatic birth happens when a mother feels terrified, overwhelmed, or in severe physical danger during labor and delivery, which affects about one in three women. Up to twenty percent of mothers develop birth related post traumatic stress disorder afterward, causing painful flashbacks and extreme fear. Using alcohol, tobacco, or drugs during pregnancy affects about five percent of mothers and often happens alongside depression or anxiety. Untreated drug or alcohol use can cause early birth, low birth weight, infant withdrawal symptoms after birth, and delays in how the baby grows and learns.
source: Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Synthesis

content: Losing a pregnancy through miscarriage or stillbirth causes deep grief and increases the risk for long term depression and anxiety. Mental health support can easily be added into standard pregnancy clinics and local health centers. By following simple guidelines like the WHO Mental Health Gap program, local nurses and community health workers can be trained to spot warning signs early and offer effective care to support mothers and their babies.
source: Policy Center for Maternal Mental Health Synthesis

content: Emergency medical and mental health hotlines in Kenya offer immediate help during severe health crises. For emergency medical care, call the Emergency Medicine Kenya Foundation toll free at 0800 723 253 or at 0710 633 855. The Kenya Red Cross Society provides emergency support at 1199, 0700 395 395, and 0738 395 395. For suicide emergencies and severe emotional distress, call Niskize at 0900 620 800 or 0718 227 440. Befrienders Kenya provides suicide, depression, and abuse support between seven in the morning and seven in the evening at 0722 178 177.

Helplines in Kenya provide immediate protection and support for victims of domestic and sexual violence. Healthcare Assistance Kenya offers a national toll free hotline for gender based violence support at 1195. Kimbilio Trust provides specialized support for women facing violence at 1193. For immediate police intervention and security emergencies, contact the Kenya Police at 999, 911, or 112.

Hotlines in Kenya assist with sexual and reproductive health, maternal care, and child safety. Marie Stopes Kenya offers reproductive health guidance at 0800 720 005. The One2One Liverpool service provides youth and maternal reproductive health information at 1190. Child Helpline Kenya supports child protection and abuse prevention at 116. Missing Child Kenya provides help for lost or displaced children at 0800 223 344. NASCOP provides care and advice regarding HIV, AIDS, and sexually transmitted infections at 0800 724 848.

The National Authority for the Campaign Against Alcohol and Drug Abuse, known as NACADA, provides a twenty four hour toll free helpline in Kenya for individuals and families dealing with alcohol and substance abuse issues. Mothers or families needing immediate support or treatment guidance for drug and alcohol dependence can call NACADA at 1192.

Essential daily hygiene and routine care protect newborns from severe infections and support healthy growth. Healthcare providers and parents must wash their hands thoroughly with soap and water before handling the baby. Immediately after birth, the baby should be wiped clean and dry, but the first full bath must be delayed for at least twenty four hours to preserve body heat. The baby should be kept warm by wearing one or two more layers of clothes than an adult, along with a soft hat to cover the head. The mother and baby should share the same room to allow continuous rooming in and on demand feeding. Routine screening tests should be completed for eye problems, hearing issues, and newborn jaundice.

Proper umbilical cord care is necessary to prevent dangerous blood infections in the first weeks of life. The umbilical cord stump must be kept clean and completely dry, without applying any oils, ointments, powders, or traditional substances. Caregivers must know early danger signs that require urgent medical attention at a health facility. Danger signs in a young infant include poor feeding or inability to suck, fast breathing, chest indrawing, high body temperature or feeling unusually cold, extreme sleepiness, or yellow skin and eyes. Spotting these danger signs early allows for quick medical treatment and prevents severe illness.

Preterm infants are babies born before thirty seven weeks of pregnancy, while low birth weight infants weigh less than two point five kilograms at birth regardless of gestational age. Worldwide, fifteen million babies are born preterm and over twenty million are born with low birth weight each year. Prematurity and low birth weight remain the leading causes of death in newborns and children under five years old. Surrounding survival, these small infants face high risks of long term developmental disabilities such as cerebral palsy and eye damage, as well as an increased risk of adult chronic conditions including diabetes and obesity.

Preterm and low birth weight infants require extra care to maintain body heat, stabilize breathing, and grow safely. For small or premature infants, skin to skin contact, known as kangaroo mother care, should be practiced as much as possible every single day. Direct chest to chest contact keeps the small baby warm, reduces stress, stabilizes heart rate, and promotes frequent breastfeeding. Continuous skin to skin contact significantly improves survival rates for vulnerable small newborns both in health facilities and after returning home.

Immunization is a vital healthcare measure that protects infants and children against life threatening infectious diseases. Vaccines work by introducing a safe, harmless piece of a virus or bacterium to trigger antibody production and train the immune system. Timely vaccination prevents severe conditions such as measles, whooping cough, diphtheria, tetanus, polio, and tuberculosis. Beyond individual protection, childhood immunization creates community immunity to protect vulnerable individuals, reduces severe complications such as brain damage or hearing loss, and saves millions of lives globally each year.
source: Kenya National Vaccines and Immunization Program

content: The Kenya National Vaccines and Immunization Program outlines specific infant schedules starting at birth. At birth or first contact, infants receive the single dose intradermal BCG vaccine to prevent tuberculosis, along with birth dose oral polio vaccine OPV zero. At six weeks of age, infants receive oral rotavirus dose one, oral polio vaccine OPV dose one, pentavalent vaccine dose one given as an intramuscular injection into the left thigh to protect against diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, hepatitis B, and Haemophilus influenzae type b, and pneumococcal conjugate vaccine PCV ten dose one given intramuscularly into the right thigh. At ten weeks, infants receive rotavirus dose two, oral polio vaccine OPV dose two, pentavalent dose two, and PCV ten dose two.
source: Kenya National Vaccines and Immunization Program

content: The routine immunization schedule in Kenya continues through early childhood to build long lasting immunity. At fourteen weeks of age, infants receive oral polio vaccine OPV dose three, inactivated polio vaccine IPV as an intramuscular injection in the right thigh, pentavalent dose three, and PCV ten dose three. At nine months of age, children receive dose one of the measles rubella MR vaccine in the right upper arm, as well as the yellow fever vaccine in high risk counties including Baringo, Elgeyo Marakwet, West Pokot, and Turkana. At eighteen months, children receive measles rubella MR dose two in the right upper arm to complete their primary infant immunization series.
source: Kenya National Vaccines and Immunization Program

content: Infections in newborns are serious health concerns because a newborn baby has an underdeveloped immune system that cannot fight off germs effectively. Although mothers pass protective antibodies to their babies through the placenta during pregnancy, antibody levels may still be too low to stop an illness. Newborns can catch infections in three main ways. First, in the womb through the placenta, causing conditions like rubella, cytomegalovirus, or syphilis. Second, during labor and delivery through exposure to vaginal fluid or blood, causing infections like group B streptococcus or herpes. Third, after birth through contact with infected caregivers, hospital equipment, or breast milk. Early diagnosis using blood, urine, or spinal fluid tests is vital so doctors can give prompt treatment with antibiotics or antiviral medicines.

Newborn sepsis is a dangerous, life threatening bloodstream infection caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi. It is divided into early onset sepsis, which starts in the first three days of life from germs passed during birth, and late onset sepsis, which develops after three days from hospital or home exposure. Premature babies and infants with low birth weight face the highest risk. Common warning signs include listlessness, poor feeding, pale or grayish skin, unstable body temperature, rapid breathing, vomiting, and seizures. Doctors diagnose sepsis using blood cultures and spinal taps. Treatment requires immediate intravenous antibiotics, oxygen, intravenous fluids, and close monitoring in a hospital.

Hospital acquired infections occur when a newborn gets an infection while staying in a hospital nursery or intensive care unit rather than from the mother before birth. Premature infants and sick full term babies who stay in the hospital for long periods face the greatest risk, especially when using breathing tubes or intravenous lines. The most common hospital acquired infections are pneumonia, bloodstream infections, and staphylococcus skin infections. Symptoms include fever or low body temperature, poor feeding, extreme sleepiness, vomiting, or skin rashes. Thorough handwashing with soap or hand sanitizer by hospital staff and family members is the most effective way to prevent these infections.

Newborn pneumonia is a serious lung infection caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi. Early onset pneumonia occurs during or shortly after birth as the baby passes through the birth canal, while late onset pneumonia develops after seven days, most often in premature babies who require breathing tubes in neonatal intensive care units. Signs of pneumonia include fast breathing, grunting sounds, pauses in breathing, increased thick mucus, fever or low body temperature, and poor feeding. Doctors confirm pneumonia using chest x rays, blood tests, and oxygen level sensors. Treatment involves intravenous antibiotics, oxygen support, and fluid care.

Bacterial meningitis is a dangerous infection of the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord, usually resulting from bacteria spreading through the bloodstream. Common causes in newborns include group B streptococcus, E. coli, and listeria. Unlike older children, newborns rarely develop a stiff neck. Instead, warning signs include severe irritability, unusual drowsiness, poor feeding, vomiting, seizures, or a bulging soft spot on top of the skull. Doctors diagnose meningitis using a spinal tap procedure to test spinal fluid. Immediate intravenous antibiotics are critical, as untreated bacterial meningitis is fatal.

Listeriosis in newborns is a bacterial infection caused by Listeria monocytogenes, which can be acquired in the womb, during delivery, or after birth. Pregnant women can contract Listeria by eating contaminated foods such as unpasteurized dairy products, soft cheeses, raw vegetables, or prepared deli meats. The bacteria can cross the placenta, potentially leading to miscarriage, preterm delivery, or stillbirth. Symptoms in newborns can appear early within hours or days of birth, often causing sepsis symptoms, or late after several weeks, typically presenting as meningitis or sepsis. Diagnosis is confirmed by culturing blood, spinal fluid, or other bodily fluids from the newborn or mother. Treatment involves intravenous ampicillin combined with an aminoglycoside antibiotic. Prevention focuses on avoiding high-risk contaminated foods during pregnancy and practicing safe food handling.

Newborn conjunctivitis is an eye infection or inflammation caused by bacteria, viruses, or chemical reactions. Bacterial causes include Chlamydia and Neisseria gonorrhoeae passed from the mother during delivery. Chlamydial conjunctivitis usually starts 5 to 14 days after birth with swollen eyelids and pus discharge, treated with oral erythromycin or azithromycin. Gonococcal conjunctivitis starts 2 to 5 days after birth with severe eyelid swelling and thick pus, which can cause blindness if untreated; it requires hospital treatment with intravenous or intramuscular ceftriaxone or cefotaxime. Chemical conjunctivitis is a mild reaction to preventive eye drops that appears within hours and resolves in a few days. Routine post-delivery preventive measures include applying erythromycin ointment to the newborn's eyes and screening pregnant women during prenatal care.

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection in newborns is typically acquired during delivery through contact with infected genital secretions, even if the mother has no active symptoms. Symptoms usually begin between the first and third weeks of life and typically start as a rash of fluid-filled blisters on the skin, mouth, or eyes. The infection can remain localized to the skin, eyes, or mouth, or it can spread to the brain and central nervous system or cause a severe widespread multi-organ infection affecting the lungs, liver, and brain. Diagnosis is confirmed by viral cultures or PCR testing of blister samples, blood, or spinal fluid. Intravenous acyclovir is the primary treatment, supplemented by topical antiviral eye medications if the eyes are involved. Prevention includes giving pregnant women with a history of herpes oral antivirals starting at 36 weeks and performing a cesarean section if active lesions are present during labor.

Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in newborns occurs primarily during labor and delivery when the infant comes into contact with maternal blood or vaginal fluids. Most infected newborns show no immediate symptoms at birth but become chronic carriers of the virus, which increases the long-term risk of liver disease, cirrhosis, and liver cancer. Infrequently, infected infants develop mild acute hepatitis causing jaundice, listlessness, growth faltering, abdominal swelling, and clay-colored stools. Diagnosis is established through blood tests that check for viral markers and liver enzyme levels, along with liver ultrasound imaging. Prevention is highly effective: all pregnant women are screened, and infants born to HBV-infected mothers receive hepatitis B immune globulin and the first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours of delivery.

Cytomegalovirus is the most common congenital viral infection in newborns, occurring when the virus passes across the placenta from an infected mother to the fetus. Perinatal CMV can also be transmitted through vaginal fluids during birth, breast milk, or blood transfusions. While most infected infants have no symptoms, about 13 percent of congenitally infected newborns show symptoms such as premature birth, low birth weight, small head size (microcephaly), jaundice, enlarged liver and spleen, and skin bruises. Diagnosis is confirmed by detecting CMV DNA via PCR testing of urine, saliva, or blood samples taken shortly after birth. Although there is no cure, antiviral medications like ganciclovir or valganciclovir can reduce the severity of symptoms and lower the risk of progressive hearing loss.

Congenital rubella occurs when a non-immune pregnant womanContracts the rubella virus during pregnancy—especially during the first 12 weeks—and passes it to the fetus through the placenta. Maternal infection can lead to miscarriage, stillbirth, or severe multiple birth defects known as congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). Common defects of CRS include low birth weight, small head size, cataracts, retinal damage, heart defects, enlarged liver and spleen, and progressive hearing loss. Diagnosis is made using antibody tests and viral detection in blood, throat, or urine samples of the mother and infant. There is no specific cure for rubella, so management involves supportive care for specific organ defects. Prevention is achieved through routine MMR vaccination of non-pregnant individuals prior to pregnancy, as the live vaccine cannot be administered during pregnancy.
